sec.title: Background
sec.p: Traditional phase I designs aim to identify the maximum tolerated dose, assuming higher doses increase efficacy, which may not hold in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy. We present DOSET (Dose Optimization with Simultaneous Efficacy and Toxicity) evaluation, a novel adaptive design jointly modeling safety and preliminary efficacy to identify the recommended dose, minimizing patient exposure to subtherapeutic or toxic doses, informed by a phase I CAR T lymphoma trial with a small sample.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: DOSET is a two-part Bayesian adaptive design. Part 1 employs the continual reassessment method (CRM) with an initial 2 + 2 + 2 escalation across three dose levels to identify tolerable doses, allowing early stopping for excessive toxicity. Part 2 randomly assigns patients across selected doses, with ongoing CRM updates allowing dose adjustments as needed. Activity is evaluated concurrently with a Bayesian interim futility framework. Final dose selection is based on joint tolerability and activity. Simulations compared dose selection accuracy, patient allocation, and safety with the Bayesian optimal interval phase I/II design (BOIN12).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: DOSET effectively selects active and tolerable doses, allocates patients efficiently, and reliably stops when all doses are excessively toxic. Compared with BOIN12, it improves dose selection without compromising safety, maintains or enhances early stopping for futile or toxic doses, and provides greater flexibility.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: DOSET integrates dose escalation and optimization in a seamless framework, leveraging safety and efficacy data. Despite small-sample sizes, it offers an efficient and flexible approach to improve early-phase CAR T cell trials and applies broadly to non-monotonic dose–response settings, including targeted therapies and immunotherapies.

list-item.p: Introduces DOSET, a Bayesian adaptive design for optimizing doses with plateau or non-monotonic responses.
Integrates real-time safety and early efficacy data with Bayesian monitoring to guide adaptive dose decisions.
Enables bespoke design, seamless escalation, and randomized optimization, allowing MTD refinement during the trial.
Enhances ethical, patient-centered, and model-informed decision making in small early-phase trials.
Applicable beyond CAR T cell trials to immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and gene or cell therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have transformed the treatment landscape for relapsed and refractory B-cell malignancies, particularly lymphomas. Despite their success, many patients—especially those with rapidly progressive disease, Burkitt lymphoma, or central nervous system (CNS) involvement—are ineligible for or do not respond to currently licensed CAR-T cell products. Moreover, relapse after CAR-T cell therapy remains a major clinical challenge, with up to 60% of patients eventually experiencing disease progression and having limited effective treatment options.

Parallel (p)CAR19 is a next-generation CAR-T cell product engineered to address several of these limitations. It incorporates a CD19-targeted single-chain variable fragment optimized for avidity and delivers an activating and dual CD28 and 4-1BB costimulatory signals via two parallel co-receptors.1,2 Preclinical studies suggest pCAR19 enhances CAR-T cell expansion, cytokine production, metabolic fitness, and antitumor activity compared with conventional second- and third-generation CD19-directed CARs. The pCAR19 product is manufactured using the Cocoon® platform (Lonza), an automated, closed-system process designed to reduce production time, minimize manual manipulation, and enable continuous in-process monitoring—factors that may contribute to improved product consistency and efficacy.

Unlike traditional cytotoxic agents, the dose–response for CAR-T cell therapies is complex and often non-monotonic; higher doses do not always confer greater efficacy and may instead increase the risk of severe toxicity.3, 4, 5, 6, 7 Thus, the conventional goal of identifying a maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in phase I trials is often insufficient. Instead, the focus shifts to identifying a recommended phase II dose (RP2D) that balances acceptable toxicity with optimal biological activity, critical for cellular therapies like CAR-T cells.

The importance of integrating safety, preliminary efficacy, and exposure-response data for dose selection has been highlighted by Shah et al.8 MDICT Guidelines 2022,9 and the FDA PROJECT OPTIMUS project.10 Broad reviews of innovative trial designs, including in adaptive platform and cellular therapy settings, have further highlighted the growing interest in seamless dose-finding approaches that move beyond traditional toxicity-only escalation rules.11, 12, 13 Specifically, these reviews emphasize the potential of adaptive designs enabling integration of randomization and flexible modeling of multiple endpoints, aligning with regulatory guidance calling for formal dose optimization strategies to inform later-phase dosing. However, advanced model-based and adaptive designs remain uncommon in CAR T trials, with only 5.5% reported to use such approaches.14

To address the need for designs that jointly evaluate efficacy and toxicity, several Bayesian model-based approaches have been developed. EffTox15,16 was among the first to model the trade-off between binary toxicity and efficacy outcomes to identify optimal dose(s). Other methods include Wages and Tait’s joint efficacy–toxicity continual reassessment method (CRM)17 and model-assisted designs such as Bayesian optimal interval phase I/II design (BOIN12).18 The BOIN framework, introduced by Liu and Yuan,19 defines finite-sample escalation and de-escalation boundaries for toxicity, with extensions like BOIN1218 and U-BOIN20 incorporating joint toxicity and activity evaluation using a utility-based approach. More recently, BARD21 integrates dose escalation, backfilling, and adaptive randomization to improve dose exploration. Collectively, these methods reflect a shift from toxicity-only paradigms toward seamless approaches accommodating non-monotonic dose–response relationships and leveraging both safety and early efficacy in dose selection.

However, EffTox can be operationally complex, requiring careful calibration of multiple model parameters, and the current BOIN12 app implementation (https://www.trialdesign.org/) offers limited flexibility. Particularly, constraints such as fixed cohort sizes, challenges in incorporating additional adaptive features, and nonmodifiable default priors may restrict trial customization and influence early or late stopping decisions in small studies.

In this work, we propose DOSET (Dose Optimization with Simultaneous Efficacy and Toxicity) evaluation, a two-part Bayesian adaptive design that enhances dose-finding efficiency in early-phase oncology trials, inspired by a first-in-human pCAR19 trial in relapsed/refractory B-cell lymphoma. DOSET uses model-based dose escalation that transitions seamlessly into dose optimization, allowing ongoing refinement of the MTD rather than fixing it after escalation. The optimization phase randomly assigns patients among acceptable doses to mitigate selection bias, particularly when dose–efficacy relationships are uncertain or non-monotonic, with Bayesian futility and safety monitoring applied throughout. DOSET also addresses key design and operational constraints common in CAR T trials by accommodating flexible cohort sizes, asynchronous toxicity and response assessment windows, and user-specified or calibrated priors. Unlike joint toxicity–efficacy designs such as EffTox and BOIN12, which require both outcomes at each interim decision, DOSET first identifies a tolerable dose range before evaluating preliminary efficacy, accommodating different assessment timelines [e.g. dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) within cycle 1, response up to cycle 2]. We describe the design and its implementation in the pCAR19 trial and present comparative performance versus BOIN12, demonstrating DOSET’s adaptability to bespoke trial features and its ability to support data-driven, patient-centered decision-making in small-sample settings with evolving dose–response relationships.

sec.title: Overview of the seamless Bayesian dose optimization design (DOSET)
sec.p:
The DOSET design comprises two sequential parts (Figure 1A) within a seamless framework. Part 1 uses a two-stage CRM with small cohorts to identify the tolerable dose range and MTD, with early stopping for excessive toxicity. Part 2 randomly assigns patients among tolerable doses to jointly evaluate safety and preliminary antitumor activity, guiding RP2D selection. Dose assignments are guided by a Bayesian framework that continuously updates dose–toxicity and dose–efficacy relationships, enabling adaptive dose adjustments, early stopping for futility or toxicity, and joint decision making to select the RP2D as the most active dose within the tolerable dose range.Figure 1
Overview of DOSET design. (A) Conceptual schematic illustrating the structure and workflow of the DOSET design. (B) Schematic overview of the two-part seamless adaptive dose optimization (DOSET) design: dose escalation, concurrent efficacy and safety monitoring, and RP2D selection. Part 1 uses a modified two-stage CRM with an initial 2 + 2 + 2 escalation to identify tolerable doses (target 20% DLT rate). Part 2 randomizes patients among candidate doses to jointly monitor safety and efficacy, allowing adaptive dose adjustments and early stopping for futility or toxicity. The RP2D is selected as the tolerable dose with highest efficacy.
CAR, chimeric antigen receptor; CRM, continual reassessment method; DLT, dose-limiting toxicity; DOSET, dose optimization with simultaneous efficacy and toxicity; MTD, maximum tolerated dose; RP2D, recommended phase II dose.

sec.title: Application of the DOSET design to the pCAR19 lymphoma trial
sec.p: The pCAR19 trial co-delivers CD28 and 4-1BB costimulatory signals with CD19 engagement to enhance T-cell activation and persistence. Up to 18 patients will be enrolled across three dose levels (DL1-DL3). This modest sample size in an early-phase trial balances statistical rigor with practical constraints, including cost, manufacturing feasibility, and patient availability, while jointly evaluating toxicity and early efficacy to guide RP2D selection.

sec.title: Part 1: dose escalation using modified two-stage CRM
sec.p:
A modified two-stage CRM is employed to identify tolerable doses, targeting a 20% DLT rate consistent with safety goals for early-phase CAR-T cell studies.•
Stage 1: patients are enrolled in cohorts of 2 using an initial 2 + 2 + 2 escalation scheme across three dose levels, with at least 28-day staggered dosing between patients. Escalation proceeds if no DLT occurs at each dose. If no DLT occurs in the first 6 patients across DL1-DL3, enrollment may continue at DL3 until an initial MTD is identified or a first DLT occurs. The latter triggers the transition to Stage 2.•
Stage 2: each new cohort of patients are allocated to the dose level whose posterior probability is closest to the 20% target, as estimated by the CRM. Dose recommendations draw on the model outputs and any additional information deemed relevant by the Dose-Decision Committee.

The CRM model employs a one-parameter empirical model to characterize the dose–toxicity relationship:F(d,β)=dexp(β)where d represents a standardized dose-level index, commonly referred to as the skeletons.22 The slope parameter β governs the steepness of the dose–toxicity curve and is assigned a mean zero normal prior N (0, σ2), reflecting a neutral prior belief centered on the skeleton, while allowing moderate uncertainty. Prior toxicity probabilities (skeleton) can be specified for each dose level using preclinical evidence, clinical judgment, and/or the model-calibrated approach of Lee and Cheung.23 Dose level 3 is set as the prior MTD, consistent with preclinical expectations. Utilizing the getprior() function in the dfcrm R package (half-width of 0.05, indifference interval = 15%-25% around the target DLT rate) yields the following skeletons: (0.049, 0.111, 0.200). The prior variance is chosen to be minimally informative (0.52), giving each dose approximately equal prior probability of being the MTD.24
Part 2 dose optimization is triggered once six patients have been treated at the proposed initial MTD, and the model continues to recommend enrolling the next patient at that dose.

sec.title: Part 2: randomized dose expansion with continued reassessment of tolerable dose range
sec.p: Once a tolerable dose range is identified in Part 1, the design proceeds to Part 2, which evaluates safety and preliminary efficacy, measured as overall response rate (ORR), defined as percentage of patients achieving a complete or partial response one month post treatment. An ORR 50% is considered promising and 25% undesirable.8,25, 26, 27

Remaining patients, up to the maximum sample size, are randomly assigned equally among candidate doses, typically the MTD and, if applicable, one lower dose, as determined by the Dose-Decision Committee. If an imbalance occurs, an additional patient will be preferentially assigned to the dose with fewer patients. Randomization mitigates selection bias, recognizing that higher doses of CAR-T therapy are not necessarily more effective.3 Randomization uses minimization by primary CNS lymphoma subtype to account for expected differences in CAR-T response and toxicity, including complications such as tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity, which only occurs in patients with malignant CNS involvement.28

Throughout Part 2, accumulating DLT and response data are incorporated into the Bayesian adaptive dose optimization design, which continually reassesses candidate doses, updates the MTD as needed, and allows early stopping for safety or futility. The CRM is updated after every two patients and at the end of Part 2, with candidate doses adjusted accordingly if the MTD changes. If the updated MTD is dose level 1, the next two patients are assigned solely to that dose. This adaptive approach enables:•
early stopping for excess toxicity or futility (see Section ‘Practical considerations’),•
refinement of the initial MTD,•
efficient identification of the optimal dose while minimizing patient exposure to subtherapeutic or overly toxic levels.
The trial concludes when the planned sample size is reached or when prespecified stopping rules are met.

sec.title: Safety monitoring and early stopping for toxicity
sec.p: Safety is monitored throughout the trial. An early stopping rule is applied if there is strong evidence that the lowest dose is too toxic, based on a Bayesian beta-binomial safety monitoring model with a weakly informative prior Beta (0.1, 0.9).

Let t be the number of DLT events among n assessable patients at lowest dose level (DL1). The posterior distribution of the true toxicity rate p1 at DL1 is(1)p1|t,n∼Beta(a0+t,b0+n−t)with a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.9. Early termination occurs if there is >85% posterior probability that the true toxicity rate at DL1 exceeds 20%:(2)P(p1>0.2|t,n)>0.85

This stopping criterion is only applied once at least three participants at DL1 are DLT assessable. Pretabulated decision boundaries (Table 1) are provided to ensure transparency, regulatory acceptability, and ease of implementation during trial conduct.Table 1

list-item.p: No skipping of doses during escalation or de-escalation.
No escalation permitted if the observed DLT rate at the current dose level exceeds the 20% target.

sec.title: Efficacy monitoring and early stopping for futility
sec.p: Efficacy is evaluated concurrently at each dose using a Bayesian beta-binomial futility monitoring model. The binary objective response outcome at dose level d is modeled as:(3)θd|r,n∼Beta(a0+r,b0+n−r)where r is the number of responses among n assessable patients, with weakly informative prior a0 = 0.25, b0 = 0.75.

sec.title: Interim futility
sec.p: After six patients, a dose is stopped if the probability that the true response rate >25% is 0.25 (corresponding to no responders of six patients):(4)P(θd>0.25|r,n)≤0.25

sec.title: Final efficacy
sec.p: At trial completion, the number of patients per dose may vary depending on the dose-escalation pathway and observed toxicities. A dose is considered to demonstrate promising antitumor activity if:(5)P(θd>0.25|r,n)>0.60
This framework allows early termination of unpromising doses while ensuring that RP2D candidates are supported by credible early efficacy signals and acceptable tolerability.

sec.title: Final selection of the RP2D
sec.p: The RP2D is determined by jointly considering both safety and efficacy among the candidate doses that have not been stopped early for toxicity or futility and corresponds to the current MTD or a lower dose.

If >1 candidate dose remains, preference is given to the dose that is both tolerable and shows stronger efficacy. Specifically, if there is >65% probability that the higher dose improves efficacy by at least 5% compared with the lower dose, the higher dose is selected; otherwise, the lower dose may be chosen to minimize potential toxicity and increase the chance of manufacturing the target cell dose. In practice, multiple doses may be carried forward if supported by efficacy, safety, and other key secondary endpoints, including ORR at later time points (e.g. 3 months), pCAR19 expansion levels in blood, and trafficking to sites such as lymph node and cerebrospinal fluid. This approach balances maximizing efficacy while minimizing potential toxicity risks associated with higher doses. Details on the implementation of the allocation strategy and RP2D selection for Part 2 are provided in Supplementary Appendix A, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767. A schematic of the overall trial design, including the RP2D selection process, is shown in Figure 1B.

sec.title: Simulation study
sec.p: To assess the performance of DOSET, we conducted a comprehensive simulation study across a range of clinically plausible scenarios varying toxicity and activity outcomes based on the pCAR19 trial. Key performance metrics included RP2D selection accuracy, patient allocation, and early stopping probabilities.

Three dose levels (DL1-DL3) were considered, with up to 18 patients enrolled in cohorts of two during the initial escalation phase, followed by continual recruitment in the dose-optimization randomized component. The target DLT rate was set at 0.2. Sixteen scenarios were evaluated, varying the location of the most active and tolerable dose(s), including cases where higher doses may not be more efficacious (Table 2). sec.title: Comparison with BOIN12
sec.p: BOIN12 was selected as the primary comparator because it is a well-established model-assisted phase I/II design that jointly evaluates toxicity and efficacy while maintaining operational simplicity, making it well suited for CAR-T trials.29, 30, 31 Its two-stage structure aligns with the aims of DOSET and provides a pragmatic benchmark for evaluating whether DOSET’s additional features—namely seamless escalation and dose optimization, randomized allocation among candidate doses, and adaptive refinement of the MTD—offer meaningful advantages over BOIN12. Other model-based alternatives (e.g. Wages and Tait17 and EffTox15) were considered but were not practical for the motivating pCAR19 trial. The Wages and Tait design17 requires response-adaptive randomization and intensive real-time monitoring, introducing substantial operational complexity without clear added benefit in small-sample settings. Similarly, EffTox requires careful prior specification and calibration of desirability or utility functions, making it substantially more complex to communicate and implement.16 In contrast, DOSET balances modeling flexibility with operational transparency by combining model-based escalation with randomized dose optimization and probability-based decision rules. This enables adaptive learning when the dose–efficacy relationship is uncertain while remaining consistent with regulatory guidance on dose optimization and evidence-based decision making in early-phase oncology trials.

DOSET was benchmarked against the two-stage BOIN12 design, which uses interval-based escalation in Stage 1 based on toxicity, followed by Stage 2 utility-based ranking of admissible doses using both toxicity and efficacy, allocating patients in cohorts of two to the highest-utility dose. Full specification of BOIN12 design parameters is provided in Supplementary Appendix B, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767.

DOSET, by contrast, does not rely on a utility function. Instead, in Part 2 it randomly assigns patients among candidate doses while jointly assessing safety and efficacy, allows refinement of the MTD, and permits early stopping for safety or futility. Interim analyses can be scheduled flexibly to balance feasibility, resource use, and statistical efficiency.32

Simulations with 1000 replicates assessed key performance metrics, comparing DOSET and BOIN12 via their metric differences: (i) probability of correct selection (PCS) of the RP2D: the percentage of trials correctly identifying the optimal tolerable dose—the dose with the highest desirable efficacy, exceeding the lower dose (if any) by ≥5%; (ii) percentage of patients treated at the true RP2D; and (iii) percentage of patients treated at doses above the true MTD.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Results for toxicity scenarios S1-S4, and efficacy scenario E1, assuming no correlation (ρ = 0) are presented in Supplementary Table C.1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767, using the default BOIN12 efficacy threshold P (πE < 0.25 | data) < 0.9 (BOIN12-1), to define a “GO” decision. Results based on additional scenarios with moderate toxicity–efficacy correlation (ρ = 0.2) and an alternative BOIN12 efficacy threshold (BOIN12-2) are presented in Supplementary Tables C.1-C.8 and Figure C.1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767. We first compared results assuming ρ = 0, then evaluated robustness under ρ = 0.2.

sec.title: Dose selection accuracy
sec.p: Under the assumption of no correlation between efficacy and toxicity (ρ = 0), DOSET demonstrated superior performance across most efficacy–toxicity scenarios. When a true RP2D existed, DOSET correctly identified it in 46%-66% of simulated trials versus 40%-63% for BOIN12. In scenarios where all tolerable doses were inactive, DOSET correctly selected “No dose” in 43%-66% of trials, while BOIN12 achieved only 4%-30%. DOSET also consistently showed higher accuracy when the RP2D was at higher doses.

Figure 2 (similarly in Figure 3A) compares the PCS across sixteen scenarios: DOSET outperformed BOIN12 in 87.5% of cases, with substantial PCS gains (>5%) in 43.8% of scenarios (dark green). In cases with similar efficacy observed at two tolerable doses, DOSET preferred the lower dose, aligning with clinical goals of minimizing toxicity. The design exhibited slightly improved performance in seven scenarios (43.8%; light green), and slightly worse performance in one scenario (6.3%; light red). Only one scenario (E4 × S2) demonstrated a notable decline in PCS (13%), where all doses were highly efficacious, but the lower dose levels exhibited similar efficacy and the MTD was DL2. This likely reflects the generally more conservative tendency to favor lower doses of BOIN12.Figure 2
The differences in the PCS between DOSET and BOIN12, under different combinations of safety and efficacy scenarios, with efficacy–toxicity correlation coefficient ρ of 0 and 0.2. The color gradient shows both the magnitude and direction of performance differences: darker green indicates greater DOSET advantage, while light green indicates greater BOIN12 advantage.
BOIN12, Bayesian optimal interval phase I/II design; DOSET, dose optimization with simultaneous efficacy and toxicity; PCS, probability of correct selection.

Compared with Supplementary Figure C.1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767, DOSET’s advantage was even greater when BOIN12 used a relaxed efficacy threshold, increasing the risk of suboptimal selections. Similar trends held under moderate toxicity–efficacy correlation (ρ = 0.2). Overall, DOSET provides more accurate RP2D selection than BOIN12, regardless of whether the dose–response relationship is monotonic or complex.

sec.title: Proportion of patients at RP2D
sec.p:
Across all scenarios, DOSET achieved a comparable proportion treated at the RP2D relative to BOIN12, with differences generally within ±5% (Figure 3B), indicating similar performance in patient allocation.Figure 3

sec.title: Proportion of patients overdosed
sec.p: Controlling patient exposure to excessively toxic doses is a key priority in early-phase trials. Across all scenarios, DOSET maintained a safety profile comparable to BOIN12, with overdosing differences generally within ±5% (Figure 3C). Both designs reliably stopped trials when all doses were highly toxic, with mean differences of fewer than one patient, indicating DOSET preserves safety while allowing dose exploration.
Overall, the design provides a strong balance between caution and exploration, offering safety performance that is comparable to BOIN12.

sec.title: Early stopping probability for futility or safety
sec.p: According to Supplementary Tables C.1-C.4, Bayesian futility monitoring in DOSET allowed early discontinuation of suboptimal doses in up to 13% of trials under S1 scenarios, reducing patient exposure to ineffective treatments. Early stopping for toxicity ranged 0%-17% in S1-S3 and exceeded 86% in S4, effectively safeguarding patients. Unlike DOSET, BOIN12 evaluates efficacy more frequently and its overall stopping probability reflects all interim and final decisions. DOSET showed >30% higher PCS than BOIN12 for selecting no dose in E1 × S1, E2 × S1, E3 × S1, and E3 × S2, demonstrating earlier and more appropriate trial termination when no effective dose exists.

sec.title: Summary of comparison with BOIN12
sec.p: Overall, DOSET demonstrated robust performance, outperforming BOIN12 in RP2D selection in 87.5% (14 of 16) of scenarios. It effectively controlled overdosing, enabled timely early stopping, and reliably identified the true RP2D, even when lower doses were highly toxic or no optimal dose existed. These advantages persisted under moderate efficacy–toxicity correlation (ρ = 0.2) (Figure 3D-F), underscoring DOSET’s superior adaptability and decision making in complex dose–response settings.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study introduces DOSET, a novel two-part Bayesian adaptive design for early-phase CAR-T cell therapy trials. By jointly evaluating safety and preliminary efficacy, the design selects an RP2D that balances tolerability with biological activity while accommodating the non-monotonic dose–efficacy relationships common in CAR-T therapies. With only ∼5.5% of CAR-T trials having used advanced model-based or model-assisted trial designs,14 DOSET’s implementation in the pCAR19 trial—with integrated safety monitoring, futility assessment, and randomization—represents an important methodological step forward.33

DOSET integrates a modified CRM in Part 1 with randomized allocation and interim analyses in Part 2 that simultaneously monitor safety, update the MTD, and assess efficacy, providing a seamless and adaptive dose-selection approach that maximizes information from small cohorts, critical given the high cost of CAR-T cell therapies. This structure enables early stopping for toxicity or futility, real-time dose–toxicity model updates, and data-driven decisions as outcomes accrue, enhancing both scientific rigor and ethical conduct. Simulation results demonstrate strong operating characteristics, with high probability of selecting a dose that is both safe and active while minimizing exposure to ineffective or harmful doses, even in small samples. Performance remains robust under modest efficacy–toxicity correlation (ρ = 0.2), supporting its applicability in early-phase trials where the true relationship is often uncertain. More broadly, DOSET offers a flexible and practical design framework leveraging established joint binary toxicity–efficacy endpoints rather than introducing a new statistical model. By combining model-based escalation, randomized optimization—useful when dose–efficacy relationship may be flat or non-monotonic—and Bayesian safety and futility monitoring within a unified adaptive structure, DOSET efficiently uses accumulating data, a key advantage in CAR-T trials with limited sample sizes.34,35 Unlike BOIN12, which provides operational simplicity through pretabulated dose recommendations and minimal real-time statistical input,36 DOSET provides greater flexibility with adjustable cohort sizes, tailored interim assessments, customized stopping rules, and accommodation of complex efficacy–toxicity relationships, demonstrating superior adaptivity via bespoke design features. Implementation remains transparent via dose transition pathways37 (Supplementary Appendix D, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.107767). Though requiring ongoing statistical oversight, simulations suggest more accurate and stable performance particularly in complex dose–response settings (e.g. CAR-T cell therapy), consistent with prior evidence favoring model-based over model-assisted designs38, 39, 40, 41 and supporting improved decision-making precision.

The Part 2 randomization strategy in DOSET mitigates selection bias and enables robust comparison of multiple candidate doses. Although response-adaptive randomization could be considered, the small numbers in Part 2 and the availability of early futility stopping make the added complexity unnecessary.42 Interim assessment can be scheduled flexibly to support timely MTD updates and early stopping for safety or futility, with simulations used to assess whether additional interim looks justify the associated operational burden.32 When two doses remain competitive with similar efficacy profiles, DOSET declares a “winner” only when there is sufficient evidence that its response rate exceeds that of the lower dose by at least 5%; otherwise, the lower dose may be selected to minimize toxicity.43

Although DOSET formally models binary toxicity and early clinical response, CAR-T–specific biomarkers such as expansion, persistence, and trafficking can aid interpretation when multiple doses appear similarly safe and active. This pragmatic separation—using primary toxicity and early clinical response for formal decision making, while allowing biological readouts to contextualize the final RP2D—maintains transparency and operational simplicity. While first-in-human CAR-T trials may observe few protocol-defined DLTs, they remain essential for defining unacceptable toxicity. Accordingly, DOSET incorporates DLTs within its safety framework while allowing additional non-DLT toxicities and CAR-T–specific biomarkers to inform final RP2D selection when needed.

In conclusion, DOSET represents a methodological advance for early-phase oncology trials, combining model-based adaptivity with operational feasibility to maximize information from small cohorts and support patient-centric and evidence-based dose selection ensuring ethical and efficient trial conduct. Beyond CAR-T therapy, DOSET is applicable to other therapeutic areas where monotonic dose–efficacy assumptions may not hold and traditional model-assisted or rule-based designs underperform, including targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and cell and gene therapies. Wider adoption of flexible adaptive designs such as DOSET could accelerate development of novel therapies, strengthen early-phase decision making, and ultimately improve patient outcomes.

sec.title: Data availability
sec.p: This study did not involve the use of clinical or patient-level data. All operating characteristics and results were generated from simulated datasets. The simulation study was conducted using R version 4.3.1, and the corresponding code is available from the author upon reasonable request.
